newsitem.title: JAPAN: Australian dlr still attractive to Japan investors.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr still attractive to Japan investors.

text.p: The Australian dollar has been bloodied after its recent plunge against the yen, but it still holds charms for Japanese investors and is unlikely to fall much more in the short term, Tokyo dealers say.

Most agree that this week's battering of the currency, taking it down more than three yen since Monday, is a temporary adjustment, and that the issuance of dual-currency bonds that has fuelled its recent surge will continue.
"What we saw (this week) was long liquidations by international funds who just bailed out," said Kenneth Landon, a senior currency strategist with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"We're still seeing quite a lot of good issuance of dual-currency bonds. Overall, I don't think the big picture's really changed that much," he added.

This week's selling, which took the Aussie from a four-year high of 93.80 yen and a six-year high of US$0.8212 on Monday, began with profit-taking and stop-loss sales on Tuesday and picked up steam after comments on Tuesday night by former Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) governor Bernie Fraser, who suggested there was room for lower interest rates.

These comments spooked the market into believing a rate cut could be imminent and set off heavy selling for the Australian currency. By late trading on Thursday, it was clinging to around 89.76 yen and $0.7963, up slightly from earlier lows.

Tokyo dealers said there was cause for optimism in the fact that the Australian dollar had managed to hold its own above a key technical support point of 89.00 yen, suggesting that the fall had been a necessary, if painful, adjustment.

"People have been bullish on the Aussie for a long time and were just using the excuse of interest rates to sell off their long positions. It will gradually go up now, but not with the speed of recent weeks," a dealer with HSBC Midland bank said.

He said, and other dealers agreed, that Japanese investor support for the Australian dollar was likely to continue. Their appetite for dual-currency bond issues this year has led to persistent buying of the Australian unit, speeding its ascent.

Of an estimated 2.1 trillion yen ($18.5 billion) of dual-currency bonds issued in Japan from January to the end of October this year, around 80 to 90 percent were in yen/Australian dollars, underwriting sources said.

With interest rates for two- and three-year dual-currency issues -- the most common -- at around five percent compared with 0.8 percent for the most recently auctioned Japanese government two-year note, dealers said Japanese investors are likely to remain keen on the Aussie even if an Australian rate cut takes place in February as expected.
"Even if there is an easing, the interest rate differential is just too high, and Japanese government bonds are not very appealing," the Midland Bank dealer said.
The advent of the winter bonus season has sparked additional interest from Japanese individual investors, and even the fall is unlikely to daunt them much, dealers said.
"I don't think this week's drop will make that much difference to the individual investors. They're mainly looking at the yield pickup," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's Landon said.

But an Australian bank dealer was cautious, saying that if rates are eased in February to 0.5 percent, as the market expects, investor enthusiasm may start to cool as the interest rate differential shrinks. Some in the market suspect the issue of dual-currency bonds could taper off as well.
"Combined with the approach of the fiscal year-end at the end of March, and investors' desire to take profits, we could well see some heavy sales then," he said. ($1=113 yen)
